questions.question: What are the two ways to create a thread in Java?
questions.title: Two Ways to Create Threads in Java
questions.direct_answer: There are two classic ways: **extend the `Thread` class** and override `run()`, or **implement the `Runnable` interface** and pass it to a `Thread` constructor. `Runnable` is preferred because it leaves your class free to extend something else and works with thread pools. A third, modern option is `Callable`, used when the task must return a value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of fundamental thread creation mechanisms and when to use each approach in production code.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking extending Thread is the preferred approach, when composition via Runnable is better because Java doesn't support multiple inheritance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Immediately state that Runnable is preferred in production because it separates the task from the thread execution mechanism and allows the class to extend other classes.

sections.title: Two Ways to Make a Thread
sections.content:
A thread is a separate path of execution your program can run. In Java you create one in **two classic ways**.

The first way is to **extend the `Thread` class** and override its `run()` method with your work. The second way is to **implement the `Runnable` interface** — which has a single `run()` method — and hand that object to a `Thread` constructor.

The difference matters because of one Java rule: a class can extend only **one** parent. If you extend `Thread`, you've used up that single slot and can't extend anything else, like a domain class or a framework base class. `Runnable` avoids that. Your class implements the interface and stays free to extend something useful.

> Prefer `Runnable` (or a lambda) in real code. It separates the *task* from the *thread* and plugs straight into thread pools.

A newer option is `Callable`, which is like `Runnable` but its `call()` method returns a value.

sections.title: Which Path to a Thread
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[I need to run code on a thread] --> B{Do I need a return value?} B -- Yes --> C[Implement Callable] B -- No --> D{Must my class extend
another class?} D -- Yes --> E[Implement Runnable
inheritance slot stays free] D -- No, but I want clean design --> E D -- I am framework code --> F[Extend Thread
rare, only to tweak the thread] C --> G[Submit to ExecutorService] E --> G ```

sections.content:
amber|Extend Thread|~Override run()|uses single inheritance|task tied to thread|less flexible
blue|Implement Runnable|~Pass to a Thread|class free to extend|works with executors|preferred
emerald|Shared Idea|~Both define run()|start() spawns thread|run() alone = no thread|you need start()
violet|Recommendation|~Runnable wins|composition over inheritance|reusable tasks|pool-ready

sections.title: Thread vs Runnable Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Extending Thread | Implementing Runnable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inheritance | Cannot extend other classes | Free to extend other classes |
| Reusability | Thread and task tightly coupled | Task can run on any thread |
| Thread pool usage | Not suitable for ExecutorService | Works seamlessly with thread pools |
| Object semantics | Represents a thread of execution | Represents a unit of work |
| Modern practice | Rarely used in production | Standard approach for concurrent tasks |

sections.title: Creating Threads Both Ways
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **`Runnable`** in almost every production scenario: handling concurrent web requests, submitting tasks to an `ExecutorService`, or when your task class already extends a domain class like `BaseService`.

Use **extending `Thread`** only in the rare case where you need to customize the thread itself — for example, a specialized thread class with custom lifecycle hooks. In a Spring Boot app processing orders, you'd implement `Runnable` so your `OrderProcessor` can extend `BaseProcessor` and still run in a thread pool.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Extending `Thread` when composition is needed**: Freshers extend `Thread` first, then realize they also need to extend another class and have to rewrite. The code compiles but locks you into a design corner.
- **Forgetting the `new Thread(...)` wrapper**: With `Runnable`, you still have to wrap it in a `Thread` and call `start()`. The `Runnable` does not start on its own.
- **Reusing a `Thread` instance**: Calling `start()` again on a finished `Thread` throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. Each `Thread` can be started only once.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Extending `Thread`**: Creates a class that IS-A thread, uses the one inheritance slot, rarely used in production.
- **Implementing `Runnable`**: Creates a class that HAS-A task, keeps inheritance free, the preferred approach.
- **Composition over inheritance**: `Runnable` separates task logic from the thread mechanism, enabling reuse.
- **`ExecutorService` compatibility**: `Runnable` works seamlessly with thread pools; raw `Thread` objects do not.
- **`start()` is always required**: Both approaches need `new Thread(...).start()` to spawn a real OS thread.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: There are two main ways to create a thread in Java. First, you can extend the Thread class and override the run method with your task logic. Second, you can implement the Runnable interface and pass that to a Thread constructor. The Runnable approach is preferred in production code because it uses composition instead of inheritance. That's important because Java doesn't support multiple inheritance, so if you extend Thread, you can't extend any other class like a business domain object or service base class. When you implement Runnable, your class is free to extend something else while still being executable in a thread. In a real Spring Boot service handling API requests, you'd implement Runnable for background tasks so they can extend framework classes and also work with ExecutorService thread pools. The Thread approach is really only used when you need to customize thread behavior itself, which is rare. One common mistake is extending Thread first, then realizing you need to extend another class and having to refactor everything. Always start with Runnable unless you have a specific reason to extend Thread.

questions.question: What happens if you call run() instead of start() on a Thread?
questions.title: run() vs start() on a Thread Object
questions.direct_answer: Calling `run()` directly executes it as an ordinary method on the current thread. Calling `start()` starts a new Java thread and that new thread invokes `run()`. A `Thread` object can be started only once; a second `start()` throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. Whether a Java thread maps one-to-one to an operating-system thread depends on whether it is a platform or virtual thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the critical difference between invoking a method and creating a new thread of execution.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling run() in test code and wondering why operations aren't happening concurrently or in parallel.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that start() is a native method that asks the JVM to allocate OS resources for a new thread and schedule run() on it.

sections.title: run() Is a Method Call, start() Spawns a Thread
sections.content:
Calling `run()` directly just runs the method on the **current** thread. Calling `start()` creates a **brand-new** thread and runs `run()` inside it. That single line is the whole answer — the rest is why.

`run()` is an ordinary method. If you call it yourself, the code executes top to bottom on whatever thread you're already on, synchronously. No concurrency happens at all.

`start()` is different. It's a **native method**: it asks the JVM and the operating system to create a real OS thread with its own call stack, then schedules `run()` to execute there. After `start()` returns, the original thread and the new thread run **at the same time**.

> A `Thread` can be started only once. Calling `start()` again throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

sections.title: Where run() Executes vs start()
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB M[main thread] --> C{Which call?} C -- thread.run() --> R[run executes on main
blocks until done
no new thread] C -- thread.start() --> S[JVM asks OS for a thread] S --> N[new thread runs run
main keeps going
both run together] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|start()|~Spawns a new thread|JVM then calls run()|runs concurrently|once per Thread
blue|run()|~Plain method call|same thread|no concurrency|like any method
emerald|The Trap|~Calling run() directly|no new thread|sequential execution|a silent bug
violet|IllegalThreadState|~start() twice|cannot restart|one thread, one start|create a new instance

sections.title: Wrong: run() blocks on the current thread
Right: start() runs them concurrently
When This Matters in Production
sections.content:
This distinction is critical in **REST services** handling concurrent requests. If you call `run()` instead of `start()` for background work, each request blocks until its task finishes — destroying throughput while one core runs hot and the rest sit idle.

The only time you'd call `run()` directly is in a **unit test**, where you want the task to execute synchronously on the test thread so timing doesn't make the test flaky. In production code that needs concurrency, `start()` is mandatory.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling `run()` in request handlers**: Writing `new Thread(task).run()` in a controller looks asynchronous but blocks the request thread completely.
- **Expecting ordered output**: With `start()`, output from different threads interleaves. That's correct behavior, not a bug.
- **Calling `start()` twice**: Reusing a finished thread by calling `start()` again throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. A `Thread` goes from NEW to RUNNABLE only once.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`run()` is a regular method**: Calling it directly executes on the current thread, with no concurrency.
- **`start()` creates a new thread**: It's a native method that asks the OS to allocate a fresh thread of execution.
- **Thread states**: `start()` moves the thread from NEW to RUNNABLE, then the scheduler invokes `run()`.
- **Parallel execution**: Only `start()` lets tasks run at the same time on different cores.
- **Start once**: Each `Thread` can be started only once, or it throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: If you call run instead of start on a Thread, no new thread is created at all. The run method just executes as a normal method call in your current thread, completely synchronously. It's like calling any other method on an object. Only start creates an actual new thread of execution. The start method is a native method that talks to the operating system to allocate a new OS thread with its own call stack and program counter. After you call start, the JVM schedules the run method to execute in that new thread, and both threads run in parallel. This matters a lot in production. If you're building a REST service and you call run instead of start for background tasks, every request will block until the task finishes, killing your throughput. A common mistake freshers make is writing new Thread task dot run, thinking they've made it concurrent, but it just blocks. In unit tests, though, calling run directly is actually useful because you can test the task logic synchronously without dealing with thread timing. So always use start in production code when you need real concurrency.

questions.question: How do you create a thread using a lambda expression in Java 8?
questions.title: Creating Threads with Lambda Expressions
questions.direct_answer: Because `Runnable` is a functional interface, you can pass a lambda directly as the `Runnable` argument to the `Thread` constructor: `new Thread(() -> doWork()).start()`. This is the most concise way to create a thread for short inline tasks, and a method reference works too.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Runnable is a functional interface and awareness of modern Java syntax for concurrency.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that any functional interface can be replaced with a lambda, thinking lambdas are only for Stream API operations.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show all three syntaxes side-by-side: anonymous class, lambda, and method reference — explain when each is clearest.

sections.title: A Lambda Can Be a Runnable
sections.content:
A lambda is a short, inline block of code you can pass around like a value. Since Java 8, you can pass one straight to a `Thread`.

This works because `Runnable` is a **functional interface** — an interface with exactly **one** abstract method, `run()`, which takes no arguments and returns void. Any lambda that matches that shape *is* a valid `Runnable`.

The syntax is `() -> { ... }`. The empty parentheses match `run()`'s no-argument signature, and the braces hold the work. For a single statement you can drop the braces entirely.

> A lambda can read variables from the surrounding method, but only **effectively final** ones — values you don't reassign.

This is far cleaner than the old anonymous-class style, and it's perfect for short background tasks like logging or sending a notification.

sections.title: From Verbose to Concise
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[Anonymous class
new Runnable with override] --> B[Lambda
arrow then body] B --> C[Method reference
object colon colon method] A -. most boilerplate .-> C C -. cleanest when logic exists .-> C ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Runnable Lambda|~Functional interface|() arrow body|no anon class|since Java 8
blue|Pass to Thread|~Concise creation|new Thread(lambda)|.start()|readable
emerald|Method Reference|~Even cleaner|obj::process|when signature fits|reuse methods
violet|Capture|~Effectively final|locals captured|no mutation|share via fields/atomics

sections.title: Three Syntaxes for Creating Threads
When to Use Each Syntax
sections.content:
Use a **lambda** for short inline tasks of one to five lines — sending an event, updating a cache, writing an audit log: `new Thread(() -> auditLogger.log(userId)).start()`.

Use a **method reference** when you're delegating to an existing method that matches `Runnable`'s signature — it reads cleanest when the logic already lives somewhere.

Use an **anonymous class** only when you need to override more than `run()`. If a lambda body grows past ten lines, extract it into a proper `Runnable` class so it stays readable.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Capturing a mutable variable**: A lambda can only capture **effectively final** locals. Trying to capture a changing loop counter is a compile error.
- **Passing arguments to a method reference**: `service::processOrder(123)` is invalid — use `() -> service.processOrder(123)` instead.
- **Cramming logic into a lambda**: A ten-plus-line lambda hurts readability. Extract it into a named `Runnable` class.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Functional interface**: `Runnable` has exactly one abstract method, making it lambda-compatible since Java 8.
- **Lambda syntax**: `() -> { code }`, where the empty parens match `run()`'s no-argument signature.
- **Variable capture**: A lambda can read effectively final variables from the enclosing scope.
- **Method reference**: Use `::` when delegating to an existing method that matches the signature.
- **No return value**: `run()` returns void, so the lambda body can't return anything.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: You can create a thread using a lambda expression because Runnable is a functional interface with exactly one abstract method. Just pass a lambda directly to the Thread constructor. The lambda syntax is open paren close paren arrow, then your code. For example, new Thread of a lambda that prints something, then dot start. The empty parentheses match the run method's no-argument signature. If it's a one-liner, you can skip the curly braces. This is way more concise than the old anonymous inner class approach, where you had to write new Runnable with the whole override block. You can also use a method reference if you're just delegating to an existing method. The lambda can capture variables from the surrounding scope as long as they're effectively final, which means you can read them but not reassign them. Use lambdas for short inline tasks like logging or sending notifications. If the logic is complex or more than ten lines, extract it to a proper Runnable class instead, because readability matters more than brevity. And in real applications, submit the lambda to an ExecutorService rather than creating raw threads.

questions.question: What is Callable and how does it differ from Runnable?
questions.title: Callable vs Runnable in Java
questions.direct_answer: `Callable` is like `Runnable`, but its `call()` method **returns a value** and can throw checked exceptions. You submit it to an `ExecutorService` with `submit()`, which returns a `Future` — a claim ticket you call `get()` on later to retrieve the result.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how to get results back from concurrent operations and handle exceptions in threads.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing how to retrieve the value from a Callable, or not understanding that Future.get() blocks until the result is ready.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Future.get() blocking behavior and mention timeout options like get(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) to avoid hanging forever.

sections.title: Callable Is a Task That Returns a Value
sections.content:
`Callable` is a task that returns a value. That's the whole difference from `Runnable`, which returns nothing.

The key piece is the **`call()` method**: it returns a generic type `T` and can throw checked exceptions. That makes it right for work like database queries, REST calls, or file parsing — operations where you need the result and might hit an error.

You submit a `Callable` to an **`ExecutorService`** using `submit()`, which immediately returns a **`Future`**. Think of the `Future` as a **claim ticket**: the task runs in the background, and you call `get()` later to collect the result.

> `Future.get()` **blocks** the calling thread until the result is ready. Submit all your tasks first, then call `get()`, or you lose the concurrency.

sections.title: Submit, Work, Then Collect
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Your code
    participant Ex as ExecutorService
    participant W as Worker thread
    App->>Ex: submit(callable)
    Ex-->>App: Future (claim ticket)
    Ex->>W: run call()
    App->>App: do other work
    App->>App: future.get() blocks here
    W-->>Ex: result ready
    Ex-->>App: returns the value
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Runnable|~run() to void|no checked exc|execute()|no result
blue|Callable|~call() to T|throws checked exc|submit() to Future|returns a value
emerald|Future|~Holds the result|get() blocks|isDone()/cancel()|exceptions surfaced
violet|Pick|~Need result/exc?|yes - Callable|no - Runnable|both pool-friendly

sections.title: Callable vs Runnable
sections.content:
| Aspect | Runnable | Callable<T> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Method signature | void run() | T call() throws Exception |
| Return value | Cannot return a result | Returns a typed result |
| Exception handling | Must catch checked exceptions internally | Can throw checked exceptions to caller |
| Executor usage | submit() or execute() | submit() only, returns Future<T> |
| Use case | Fire-and-forget background tasks | Tasks requiring a result or status |

sections.title: Callable with Future Result Retrieval
When to Use Callable vs Runnable
sections.content:
Use **`Callable`** when you need a result back: fetching profiles from a database, calling external REST APIs, or computing a value. In a service that checks shipping cost from three providers concurrently, each check is a `Callable` returning the cost.

Use **`Runnable`** for fire-and-forget side effects with no return value: sending emails, writing audit logs, refreshing caches. If the task might throw a checked exception like `IOException` that the caller should handle, `Callable` is the only choice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Blocking too early on `get()`**: Calling `future.get()` right after `submit()` blocks until the result is ready, losing all concurrency. Submit every task first, then call `get()`.
- **Swallowing `ExecutionException`**: When the `Callable` throws, `get()` wraps it. Always call `getCause()` to recover the real error.
- **No timeout on `get()`**: A plain `future.get()` can hang forever. Use `get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` to fail fast.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`call()` returns a value**: Unlike `run()`, which returns void, `call()` returns a typed result `T`.
- **Checked exceptions allowed**: `call()` declares `throws Exception`, so it can propagate `IOException` without catching.
- **`Future<T>` pattern**: `submit()` returns a `Future` immediately; the result comes later via `get()`.
- **`Future.get()` blocks**: It suspends the calling thread until the task completes — plan the call order.
- **Timeout protection**: `get(timeout, TimeUnit)` avoids hanging if a task is stuck or slow.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Callable is like Runnable but designed for tasks that return a result. Instead of a run method that returns void, Callable has a call method that returns a typed value and can throw checked exceptions. You use it with an ExecutorService by calling submit, which gives you back a Future object immediately. The Future is like a claim ticket. The task runs in the background, and you call future dot get to retrieve the result when you need it. The important thing to know is that get blocks the current thread until the result is ready, so you don't want to call it right after submit, or you lose all concurrency. The pattern is submit all your tasks first, do other work, then call get on each Future at the end. In production, always use the timeout version of get so your code doesn't hang forever if a task gets stuck. If the Callable throws an exception, get wraps it in an ExecutionException, so you call getCause to unwrap the actual error. Use Callable when you need results back from concurrent operations, like fetching data from multiple APIs or databases. Use Runnable for fire and forget tasks like logging or sending notifications.

questions.question: What is an ExecutorService and why is it preferred over creating threads directly?
questions.title: ExecutorService vs Raw Thread Creation
questions.direct_answer: `ExecutorService` separates task submission from the way tasks are executed and provides lifecycle methods such as `shutdown()`. Many implementations use a reusable thread pool, but the interface does not guarantee a fixed or bounded pool. You must choose an executor and queue policy that match the workload.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands production-grade thread management and the problems with creating raw Thread objects.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a new Thread for every incoming request in a web service, which causes resource exhaustion under load.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the Executors factory methods like newFixedThreadPool, explain bounded vs unbounded pools, and mention shutdown vs shutdownNow.

sections.title: A Thread Pool You Submit Tasks To
sections.content:
**`ExecutorService`** is an interface for submitting tasks, obtaining results, and controlling executor shutdown. It separates *what the task does* from *which thread runs it*.

A fixed-thread-pool executor reuses a bounded number of worker threads, so it avoids creating one platform thread per task. Other implementations behave differently: a cached pool can create more workers as demand grows, a single-thread executor serializes tasks, and a virtual-thread-per-task executor creates a virtual thread for each task. Therefore `ExecutorService` itself does not mean 'fixed pool' or 'bounded load.'

Choose the implementation, queue capacity, rejection behavior, and shutdown policy deliberately. Always stop an owned executor with `shutdown()` and wait or escalate with `shutdownNow()` according to the application's lifecycle.

sections.title: Tasks Queue, Threads Reuse
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S[submit task] --> Q[task queue] Q --> P{free thread
in pool?} P -- Yes --> T[worker runs task
then returns to pool] P -- No --> W[task waits in queue] T --> Q W --> P ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Task submission|~Runnable or Callable|separate work from execution|Future where requested|executor controls policy
blue|Implementations vary|~Fixed workers, cached, scheduled, virtual threads|queue behavior differs|not always a pool|not automatically bounded
emerald|Load policy|~Choose concurrency and capacity|rejection or backpressure|downstream limits|observe failures
violet|Lifecycle|~Owner shuts down|stop accepting work|await completion by policy|shutdownNow is best-effort interruption

sections.title: Wrong: a new thread per task
Fixed workers with an explicit shutdown policy
When to Use ExecutorService
sections.content: Use an owned `ExecutorService` when code needs to submit multiple tasks under one scheduling and shutdown policy. Fixed, cached, scheduled, work-stealing, and virtual-thread executors have different behavior; select one from task type, downstream capacity, queueing, and cancellation needs. A directly created Thread can still fit a deliberately dedicated lifecycle. In frameworks such as Spring, use the framework-managed executor when appropriate and inspect its configuration rather than assuming one pool model.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming one platform-thread stack size:** reservation and commitment depend on JVM, options, platform, and thread type.
- **Calling fixedThreadPool fully bounded:** worker count is fixed, but its usual queue is unbounded.
- **Treating shutdownNow as force:** it requests interruption and returns tasks that never started; tasks must cooperate.
- **Losing interruption during shutdown:** restore the current thread's status after cleanup.
- **Saying execute loses every exception:** it provides no Future; an uncaught failure follows the worker's uncaught-exception handling.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Purpose**: submit tasks without tying them to manually created `Thread` objects.
- **Lifecycle**: `shutdown()`, `awaitTermination()`, and `shutdownNow()` help an owner stop the executor.
- **Not always a pool**: behavior depends on the implementation.
- **Not automatically bounded**: some executors or queues can grow with load.
- **Design choice**: choose worker model, queue capacity, rejection, and task type for the workload.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`ExecutorService` is the Java concurrency abstraction I use to submit `Runnable` or `Callable` tasks without hard-wiring each task to a new `Thread`. It also gives me `Future` results and an explicit shutdown lifecycle.

A common implementation is a fixed thread pool, which reuses a chosen number of platform threads. That can bound active concurrency, but the usual factory also uses an unbounded work queue, so it does not by itself bound queued work. Other executors use a single worker, grow workers, schedule tasks, or run each task on a virtual thread. I therefore would not say every `ExecutorService` is a fixed pool. In production I choose the executor and queue policy for the workload, handle task rejection where relevant, and shut down an executor that my component owns.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app processing order requests with multiple threads
familiarity_anchors: a pool of taxi drivers vs hiring a new driver per trip
a team of reps vs firing and hiring per call
a thread pool at a call center
speakable_v2.hook: It's like hiring a new worker for every order. By the time they're ready, the work's basically done.

beats.text: An `ExecutorService` manages a pool of worker threads. You submit tasks, and the pool reuses its threads instead of making new ones. Calling submit hands back a `Future`, and that Future holds the eventual result of a Callable.
Making an OS thread costs real money, with system calls plus memory. If your app spins a new thread per request, that's a thousand creations for a thousand requests. A pool skips all that waste.

items: `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n)`: exactly n threads, and extra tasks wait in a queue.
`Executors.newCachedThreadPool()`: spins threads as needed and reuses idle ones.
`Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()`: just one thread, so tasks run in order.

beats.text: Here's the non-obvious trap. The `ExecutorService` needs a shutdown call. If you submit work with `executor.submit(() -> compute())` and forget, the pool threads keep the JVM alive forever.

items: Forget the shutdown call and the JVM won't exit. That's a classic leak.
An unbounded cached pool under heavy load can spawn thousands of threads and blow up memory.

speakable_v2.cap: So lean on pools in production. Raw `Thread` creation's just for learning, and you won't ship it.

questions.question: What is a daemon thread in Java and when would you use one?
questions.title: Daemon Threads in Java
questions.direct_answer: A daemon thread is a Java thread that does not keep the JVM alive. When no started non-daemon thread remains, the JVM may exit even if daemon threads still have work. Set daemon status before `start()`. Do not use daemon threads for work that must flush, save, or complete reliably.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JVM lifecycle and how threads affect application shutdown behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting daemon status after calling start(), which throws IllegalThreadStateException and has no effect.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete production example like a health check monitor that polls metrics every 5 seconds but shouldn't block application shutdown.

sections.title: A Background Thread That Won't Block Shutdown
sections.content:
A **daemon thread** is a background-support thread that does not keep the JVM alive. The distinction is about JVM termination, not thread priority or automatic cleanup.

When all started non-daemon threads have finished, the JVM may terminate while daemon threads are still running. Their `finally` blocks are not a reliable shutdown mechanism, so important writes, transaction completion, and log delivery should not depend on a daemon thread getting one last chance.

Call `setDaemon(true)` before `start()`; changing daemon status after start throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. Daemon threads can fit optional support work, but managed executors and explicit shutdown hooks are clearer for most application services.

sections.title: JVM Exit and Daemon Threads
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[App runs] --> B{Any user thread
still alive?} B -- Yes --> A B -- No --> C[JVM runs shutdown hooks] C --> D[Daemon threads killed abruptly
no finally blocks] D --> E[JVM exits] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Daemon Thread|~Background helper|setDaemon(true)|before start()|dies with the JVM
blue|User Thread|~Default|keeps the JVM alive|JVM waits for it|non-daemon
emerald|JVM Exit|~When daemons die|all user threads done|daemons killed abruptly|no finally guarantee
violet|Use For|~Support tasks|monitoring, cleanup|cache eviction|never critical work

sections.title: Creating and Using a Daemon Thread
When to Use Daemon Threads
sections.content:
Use **daemon threads** for non-critical background support: a health check polling status every few seconds, a cache cleaner removing stale entries, log rotation, or a metrics collector. In a REST API, a daemon thread might log queue depth every ten seconds.

Use **user (non-daemon) threads** for work that must complete: processing an order, writing to the database, or sending a confirmation. If a payment thread were a daemon, shutdown could interrupt it mid-transaction and corrupt data.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Setting daemon after `start()`**: `setDaemon(true)` after the thread starts throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. It must be set before `start()`.
- **Using a daemon for critical work**: If the JVM shuts down, the daemon is killed mid-operation, risking corruption or an incomplete transaction.
- **Expecting cleanup to run**: Daemon threads are terminated abruptly, so `finally` blocks don't execute. Use a JVM shutdown hook for guaranteed cleanup.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Daemon thread**: does not keep the JVM alive.
- **Termination**: JVM shutdown may stop it before its work or cleanup finishes.
- **Configuration**: call `setDaemon(true)` before `start()`.
- **Wrong use**: durable writes, transactions, or required log flushing.
- **Better control**: managed executors plus an explicit application shutdown path.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A daemon thread is a thread that does not prevent JVM shutdown. If every started non-daemon thread has finished, the JVM can exit even though daemon threads are still running. For example, an optional in-memory metrics sampler could be daemon work because losing its final sample is acceptable. A thread writing an audit record should not be daemon work, because shutdown may stop it before the record is stored.

The daemon flag must be set before `start()`. For most application services I prefer an executor owned by the application and shut it down explicitly, because that gives required tasks a controlled chance to finish.

familiarity_anchors: a cleaner who leaves when the office closes
a background process that auto-closes with the app

speakable_v2.hook: Daemon threads are the JVM's quiet helpers. They run in the background and die the moment real work ends.

beats.text: A daemon thread runs in the background, and the JVM may terminate without waiting once no non-daemon thread remains. You mark one with `setDaemon(true)` before `start()`. Do it after the thread starts and you'll get an `IllegalThreadStateException`.

Some jobs should run only while the app lives, yet never block its exit. A health poller, a cache cleaner, an optional in-memory sampler — none of them should keep the JVM hanging once the real work's done.

items: User threads are non-daemon. They keep the JVM alive until they finish. That's the default.
Daemon threads get killed automatically once the last user thread ends. The GC runs as one.

beats.text: Here's the sharp edge. Daemon threads don't run their finally blocks on shutdown. So open files or DB connections in a finally won't close. Critical cleanup belongs in a JVM shutdown hook instead.

items: Never lean on a daemon thread for must-finish work, like writing a final record.
`setDaemon(true)` has to come before `start()`, or it throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

speakable_v2.cap: So daemon threads suit quiet background jobs that vanish on exit. Anything that must finish stays a user thread.
